title: Infrared view of the Rho Ophiuchi star-forming region
caption: The Rho Ophiuchi star-forming region, imaged by NASA's WISE
celestial: Rho Ophiuchi · constellation Ophiuchus · about 400 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: NASA's Wide-field Infrared Explorer, WISE, a space telescope rather than one of ESO's own, observed the Rho Ophiuchi star-forming region in infrared light.

The colors carry a clear meaning. Blue and cyan stand for 3.4- and 4.6-micrometer light, which mostly comes from stars. Green and red show light at 12 and 22 micrometers, which is mostly given off by dust. So the image separates the region into its stars and the dust clouds among which they are forming.

That split matters because star-forming regions are dusty places. Dust blocks visible light, hiding many young stars, but it also glows in the infrared when warmed. Longer infrared wavelengths therefore trace the dust itself, while shorter ones pick out the stars. The official caption offers few further details.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (235.57 x 231.40 arcminutes) and distance (400 light years), the frame spans roughly 27 × 27 light-years. Its light set out about 400 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This infrared image comes from NASA's WISE. Blue and cyan represent 3.4 and 4.6 micrometers, mostly starlight, while green and red represent 12 and 22 micrometers, mostly glowing dust.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, so the colors are assigned to wavelengths we cannot see.
